utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you're pointing to an area between Gornja Jakupovici and Donja Jakupovici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far was it from where you lived to Kozarac? In kilometres, how far was it from your house to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Approximately seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how many kilometres would it be from your house to the town of Prijedor? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Around 20, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the map, we see a red line that appears to be a principal road. Was there a road that went from Omarska to Prijedor, passing through Kozarac and Kozarusa, or next to them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure. We see the red line on the map. Was there a road that went from Omarska passing through Kozarac on into the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: There was the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road, the principal road, the one that was usually used, and then the road forked off to Omarska. You can see it here. And there was a rail line here from Banja Luka for Omarska through Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And also, if you were travelling from Omarska to Prijedor, would you take that road through Kozarac to get to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The bus went from Omarska through Jakupovici, Kamicani, Kozarac, and then on to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. On that day, you said you were at home, and the announcement was that if the -- that the checkpoints had to be removed from the road, the Banja Luka Road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did they say would happen? What else do you remember about the announcement on the radio? What would happen if the checkpoints were not removed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they said that unless these barricades were removed on the road, they said that they would apply military force to remove them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there a checkpoint or a barricade in Jakupovici on the main road that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you a member of any armed group defending that area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of any of the armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, I did not have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about your father? To your knowledge, was he a member of an armed group, did he participate at that checkpoint or barricade?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He wasn't there at the barricade. At the moment when the attack was carried out, he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He was at a neighbour's place. The name of the neighbour was Ahmed Colic. That may have been perhaps a hundred metres from our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you heard the announcement on the radio, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I was still at home, having lunch, as I've said, and then I went out, and as neither my mother nor my father were at home, I was alone. So I went to my aunt's house, where I found my mother. And I'm not sure how much time elapsed, but then the shooting began. And when the shooting began, I was really scared because shells started falling. Nothing like that had ever happened to me previously. I found my mother there, and there were a number of other women there and my relations. Some were there in my aunt's basement. Not much time elapsed before my father came, too, and then after perhaps 10, 15, 20 minutes, my cousin, my two cousins, Sakib Poljak and Sabid Poljak, arrived, and some other neighbours. And they said that we had to run, leave the village, that the army attacked the barricade and that a tank drove through the barricade in the direction of our houses. They said we had to leave the basement and run towards Kozarac because they hoped that there, it would be safer. This was all happening very quickly. No one really managed to collect any of their belongings. We just took off for Kozarac. We didn't use the road. We went off the road towards Gornja Jakupovici and then across fields and through forests. We gradually tried to reach Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to stop and go back and ask you some questions about what you've just told us. You said that shooting started and shelling. Can you describe to us exactly what you heard and saw.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That was -- how should I put it? Suddenly, the shooting came, and then shells started falling, the shelling began. You had the impression they were coming from all possible directions. They fell on fields and on houses. It all happened at once. So you heard the sounds of shooting, and then the shelling began. And I don't think the shelling stopped before Wednesday. Shells were falling all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're talking now about the 24th of May, and do you remember what day of the week that was?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say that the shells were coming and falling everywhere, how much time was there between, on average, to your best estimate, between when you would hear the explosions of shells?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, every two or three minutes. I don't know. I can't remember exactly. I just know that shells were falling all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was being shelled? Did it seem to you that any particular area was targeted? What was there to be hit?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They targeted everything, even when we started to run across the fields. There were no houses there, but still also those areas were being shelled. The forest, too. Maybe they were watching us with binoculars, but they were shelling all the areas. I had the impression that shells were falling literally all over the place. So we retreated slowly, and as soon as we heard a shell whistle by, we would just run for shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were at your aunt's house, I believe. How far was that from the barricade that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: About 800 metres, approximately, a kilometre perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said someone came and told you that you had to retreat, that the army had attacked. I think you said it was your cousin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You didn't yourself see what happened at the checkpoint or barricade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That's correct. You couldn't see it from my house because there's a forest, a grove, between. So it was impossible to see. You had to be standing very close, perhaps 200 or 300 metres from the barricade, to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did anyone who was present at the barricade tell you at any time what happened there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When we were retreating, we reached a forest, and we paused to get some rest. There was a creek there. And the place was quite sheltered. And my cousin told me there what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did he tell you had happened at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They were there, and suddenly, a tank drove up from the direction of Omarska. And in the spot where the barricade was, perhaps two or three hundred metres from there, there is a creek and a forest. And as the tank drove across the bridge, it was followed by a group of soldiers who then lined up beside the tank, and they started shooting. The shooting began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your cousin tell you whether the people at the checkpoint or barricade fired back at the tank or at the soldiers that were coming from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they did fire back a bit. And then they fled, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he say why they fled after just firing back a little bit?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They had to. They ran to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you ran out of your aunt's house and went to the woods. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We got some rest in the forest and then gradually and very slowly, we kept on retreating because we no longer knew -- the area was not safe. It had mixed population. There were Serb houses there and Muslim houses, too. So slowly we reached Kamicani. My mother, my father, and I split up from the remaining part of the group, our neighbours, and we went to Brdjani, to the house of my sister-in-law's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is this still Sunday? Approximately what time was it when you got to Brdjani? What time of day, afternoon or evening?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When we reached Kamicani, it was already evening. The sun was beginning to set. I'm not sure what time it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So did you and your parents go to your sister-in-law's father's house?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you said that was in Brdjani. Is that shown on the map? Can you point to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible to focus that a bit.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've pointed to the first blue dot, basically to the right, to the east of Kozarac. How long did you stay in Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We stayed in Brdjani until Tuesday afternoon, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During that time, was -- the area of Brdjani, could you still hear explosions? Was there shelling in that area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling. We stayed in the basement for the whole time. A young man I know, he's one year younger than I am - he went to primary school with my cousin - he was hit in the face by a shrapnel. They kept shelling the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say he was hit in the face, was his wound serious?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was not a serious wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after the two days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Someone arrived. The basement was full of people seeking shelter. I didn't know most of those people. They were from that area. They came over. Someone came over and said that Kozarac had fallen and that an order had been issued to go towards Kozarac in a convoy and to surrender to the Serb authorities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did the people in the house that you were staying in do then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They went out to the road, where many people had already assembled, and then they took off for Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say, "they took off," the way it was translated, how did you travel to Kozarac? Were the people using vehicles, on foot, or a combination?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I did not go to Kozarac from Brdjani myself. But those people, they walked from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of those people?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why didn't you go with that group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your parents go with the other people?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, my parents left. My father did not want to be separated from my mother and my sister-in-law who had a baby then who was six months old, a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break now for 20 minutes. We resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, may I ask, do you feel better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please, let us know in any event if you have some problems. Don't hesitate to tell us immediately because we are aware how difficult it is for you to give us your testimony. But I think we can proceed. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: With the consent of my learned colleagues, I'm going to ask the next question in a leading manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, at that time, did you say goodbye to your parents and decide to try to make your way with a smaller group to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That's when I decided to say goodbye to my parents and to my sister-in-law's brother, too. Actually, I decided, with my sister-in-law's brother, to try to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did the two of you, then, set out towards trying to travel on foot to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That was our aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to the map that's on the machine to your left, can you just show us, when you left Brdjani, generally where you headed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could go in a little bit more towards Brdjani, focus in a little bit more towards the centre.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We set out towards Kozara, straight towards Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Kozara is the mountain, Kozara, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is the area like? What's the topography there? Is it wooded area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And tell us about that journey. What happened when you set out with your sister-in-law's brother?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We set out. I separated from my parents on the road and we set out towards Kozara. There were people there all over, women, children, elderly people. It was very chaotic. Some started out in columns. People didn't know what to do or where to go. I didn't know the area because I had never been to that area previously. I went with this young man. At nightfall, in the woods -- because that was not very far from those villages, from Brdjani. If you head down from Brdjani, very quickly you reach the foot of the Kozara, of Mount Kozara, and the woods there at the foot of it. At nightfall, there were many people there. So we simply spent the night in the woods. You could still hear sounds of shooting and shelling through the night. In the morning, when we woke up, there was another group of people assembled there and they had the same intention as we did, so we joined this group, the two of us. And I'm not sure who the leader of this group was, who led the way, who was the guide. I didn't know. We started out slowly. I didn't know where I was going. We were in the woods and the area was unfamiliar to me. So we just walked on, and we followed those other people there. We slowly made our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This group of people that you joined with in the woods, was it a military group? Was it all men? Can you describe the group that you joined to travel with? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: There were armed persons, too, in that group. There were a number of women, children, elderly people, some young people, too, persons aged 15 or 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then? Where did the group go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We went to Croatia through the woods. I didn't know the way. I just followed. That young man and I, we joined the group and we just went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened when the group was passing, going up the mountain?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We woke up in the morning. It was early. And the group started out. Several young men walked ahead of everyone else, reconnoitring the area. I remember that we crossed the road to Mrakovica. I remember clearly that we passed a memorial fountain from World War II. It was some sort of a fountain and it had a plaque on it. I can't remember what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that memorial on Kozara mountain to the partisans from World War II, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed. We sat down, and there was a forest path nearby. And whoever wanted to drink, drank water there at the fountain. So we sat down and we rested. And then some distance from us, we heard a shot. And five minutes later, someone came over and said: "Don't be afraid. It was just an accidental shot."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the group you were in. Can you give us a rough estimate about the number of people that were in that group.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. Eighty, perhaps a hundred people. Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And again, I want to ask you, did you have a weapon, or in that group did anyone give you a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I did not have a weapon. There were a couple of armed people there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after you received this report that the one shot was accidental?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Before long, we were sitting there by the path, and down there, there was a creek, some sort of a creek. And then the other side of the creek, someone started shooting. Shooting began. We were just resting there and everything was silent, and suddenly, we heard sounds of shooting in several places at once. And we started running. I turned around, and everyone started running up the hill. They didn't take the path. They just started running straight into the woods, scared by the shooting. So I started running, too. And we reached some sort of a plateau or a path. I can't remember exactly. So we stopped there, and the shooting stopped. And then someone started speaking through a loudspeaker. It must have been a military commander of sorts. And the voice said: "Do not resist. You are surrounded. Surrender immediately. We guarantee your personal safety."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When the shots were being fired, do you know if anyone in your group was hit by any of the shots?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone being hit. It took place in the morning, around 10.00 approximately. Everything was quiet and silent, and all of a sudden, this shooting occurred, and people scattered around. I didn't see anyone open fire. The people who were walking ahead were some kind of scouts, and it is possible that they saw what happened. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you heard the announcement, could you see the people that were indicating for you to surrender?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. They were calling out over the loudspeaker, telling us to surrender, and that we had been surrounded and that they would guarantee our personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And who were those people, if you saw them? Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: At that moment, we couldn't actually see anyone. We didn't see where they were, who they were. We didn't know whether we were indeed surrounded or not. We couldn't see them. We could only hear them over the megaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So what did you do? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: This young man I was with at that time said: "What should we do? We have been surrounded. I think we have to surrender." And at that moment, people started surrendering, going down towards the creek. And it was at that moment that we saw Hamid Hodza, Ekro and Eno Alic. All of these people were in our group. We saw them going down towards the creek and surrender. So the two of us decided that we should also surrender. We said, "Well, since the two of them are surrendering, I think we better surrender, too."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Those two people that you mentioned, the first you said Ekro Alic, why were you -- who was he? Why did his surrender have significance to you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He had a business of his own. Actually, both of them, Ekro and Eno, did have a shop. They were one of the wealthiest people in Kozarac. They are some distant relatives of mine. My mother's maiden name was Alic. And then there was Hamid Hodza, as well, whom I knew and who was living in Jakupovici for a while, in the area of Gornji Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Hamid Hodza, was he a hodza? Was he a religious official?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, a hodza. That's what we called them in Bosnia. He was a kind of priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you walk down to the creek and surrender?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all of us started going down towards the creek, and when we came out on to the other side of the creek, we came across a path -- actually, it was a dirt road, where we were ordered to lie down on our stomachs and put our hands behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And who were the people that were ordering you to do that? Can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The military, armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were they wearing army uniforms, police uniforms, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I remember that there were camouflage uniforms. Some wore old JNA military uniforms, the olive-green uniforms of the former JNA. As far as I could observe, there were two or three different kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you were ordered to lie on the ground, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We were at the end of the column, at the back of the column, and we were amongst the last who came down to the creek. When I lay down on the ground, somebody kicked me or hit me on my shoes or sneakers - I don't know what I was wearing at the time - and told me to stand up. And he said: "The three of you should come with me." They wanted -- he wanted us to collect the weapons that had been discarded in the woods, which is what we did. We got up and followed this man. When we got there, we saw that a group of soldiers had already inspected those weapons. They had emptied the clips. They had taken off the clips. So we collected those weapons. The man who escorted us, a soldier, was actually very friendly. He said something to the effect, "This is a very nice country, a very nice area. Why did this have to happen? Why did you do this? You didn't stand a chance to defend yourselves." He then said: "Don't you know what forces attacked you?" And I remember he mentioned special units from Belgrade and Knin. He personally was from Bosanska Gradiska. So we spent some time talking to him and collected the weapons that we found. And after that, we went down again. But while we were collecting the weapons, we heard a shot coming from the direction of the road. After we finished collecting weapons, we went down to the road and lay down on the ground again. And I remember that they were passing behind our backs and shouting that we should turn over all the jewellery, money and gold that we had, and to put them all on one pile, which is what we did again. So we spent some time lying on the ground like this. I don't remember exactly how much, but at one point in time, they ordered us to get up and place our hands behind our heads. I don't remember how we marched down, whether it was in a single file or in two-by-two column. But as we were going down, I saw traces of blood alongside the road. And all of a sudden, I saw a body of a man who was obviously dead, who had been shot in his eye. He was -- his face was covered with blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you -- did anyone tell you, who had remained in the group when you went to collect the weapons, what had happened to the man who was shot in the eye?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, obviously, we couldn't talk. It was not until we reached Benkovac where we were detained in the premises there, including the bathroom there, that people told us that apparently a Croatian passport had been found on this young man, and they said that he was a member of the ZNG, that he had come from Croatia to fight there, and that's why they executed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So where did the soldiers take you in the files? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: For a while, we walked along this dirt road until we reached the Kozara/Mrakovica Road. When we got there, they put us on to the trucks and drove us to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to turn to the map for a moment. And can you see on the map where the Benkovac barracks are? And can you point to those.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness has indicated the area marked "Benkovac" on the map. May the witness be shown two photographs, Exhibits S15-29. Perhaps I'm going to show him later but you can bring to him S15-26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Poljak, can you tell us, what was Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Benkovac used to be a training ground for young men who did not attend secondary school. For example, my sister didn't go to the secondary school, and she spent 15 days in training there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now showing you what has been marked S15-29. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it like this when I'm looking at it. Because I had never been to Benkovac before that. We were simply brought there in trucks and...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that answer. When you got to Benkovac, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They took us out of the trucks and lined us up in front of a huge stage, in three lines, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown S15-26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And again, we appreciate you being honest with us. Do you recognise or can you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The stage that you're talking about, was that indoors or outdoors?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The stage was outdoors. It was an ordinary stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: This is where we were lined in three rows and where we remained standing, with our hands behind our heads. It was very hot. It was summertime. Some people came up on to the stage, walked around a little, probably looking for someone. And at one point, five or six people were singled out from this group. I remember clearly that they had taken out Ekro Alic. Well, he was the only one I knew personally out of the six people that had been singled out from the group. So I remember him very well. We had to remain standing. We were turned, facing the stage, but still with our hands behind our heads. He was taken out and brought to a nearby building outside this building. So they probably started beating him up because we could hear his screams. We could hear him shout: "Don't do this to me. Better kill me." And this is all we heard. And after that, there was silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the group being taken to Benkovac. You said that in your group, that it was mixed, that there were men, some women and children. Were the women and children also brought to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Not to the barracks, no. The women were not brought to the barracks. There were a few underaged men who had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that when Ekro Alic was taken out, you heard his screams, and then silence. Before the silence, did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They took him out. They started beating him. We could clearly hear that. I remember very well that he said: "Don't do this to me. Better kill me." I remember this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear a shot?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you hear the shot?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you did you hear the shot?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, as soon as he uttered those words: "Don't do this to me, better kill me," at the same time -- almost at the same time, we heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that several other people were taken out from the group at the same time. Do you have any information about what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The several people who had been taken out of the group never returned. None of them ever came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did they do with you after being placed in these rows in front of the stage?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We stayed there in front of the stage for quite some time. Various people climbed on to the stage, walked around, and observed. There were many soldiers all over the place. They were shooting, singing, roasting a lamb on a pit. I don't remember what else they were doing. But at any rate, after a while, maybe one, two, or three hours later, they told us -- they allowed us to sit down. So we sat down. Somebody, I think, brought us water. And after we had been sitting like that for a while, we were transferred to some sort of bathroom or toilets, toilet area. The toilets were on the right and the bathroom was on the left, and this is where we were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the room that you were in, can you describe the dimensions by either giving us the metres or showing us the area in this room that would be equivalent to the area that you were detained in in the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Two by three, perhaps, or a bit larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many people were detained in that room with you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know the number but I remember that the room was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say it was full, how many days did you spend in that room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you able to lie down and sleep in the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We could lean a little bit to the side but we couldn't lie down. Some people leaned against the wall or next to each other. But there was not enough room for us to lie down normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like during those three days that you were there as far as food and water and other normal necessities?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They threw in some bread from time to time. A couple of times, they threw in small packages of jam into the room. It's not like they brought us breakfast, lunch, and dinner regularly, of course. But I remember that a couple of times they came and threw in some bread and these small packages of jam. That's what I remember. I think that we were given water in jerry cans. I don't remember that there was any running water in those taps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was anyone taken out of the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I remember very well that Hamid Hodza had been taken out a couple of times. He was severely beaten up. Once he returned, he wasn't even put back into the room. He remained on a small -- sitting on a small chair in the corridor. He didn't have any clothes on from the waist up. He didn't say anything. He didn't speak. He just sat quietly on the chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did his body look like from the waist up that you could see?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was all black and blue, even purple. He was all covered in black bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the three days, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Then one day, they came and told us that we should draft a list of those who were underaged. So somebody compiled such a list, and these people were picked up and taken in a bus somewhere. It was later that I heard that they had been transferred to Trnopolje because a cousin of mine was with this group of young men. That night, the rest of us were loaded on to the buses and transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before we leave the Benkovac camp, you talked about the hodza being called out and coming back with bruises. Was he the only person that you know of that was called out or were others also called out and apparently beaten?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: There were five or six other people who were subsequently captured and brought there, but I don't know their names. I mean, I don't know them. I remember that there was a young man whom they called Sova. That's all I remember, that they called him Sova. Actually, they called him out very often: "Come over, Sova." They would take him out of the room, beat him up and then bring him back again. There were a couple of people who were taken out and beaten up, but they were all subsequently returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During those three days, did you remain all that time in the bathroom or were you allowed to go out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Only those who were taken out and beaten, only these people went out. I don't remember anyone else leaving the toilet area. We stayed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So Friday -- you said the 24th of May was a Sunday, so Friday would have been the 29th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They came and they told us to go, to go away, that they would transfer us from there. We didn't know where we were going or anything. It was late in the afternoon. There was still some daylight. They came with a list of first and last names; and as they called out our names, we went outside. They made us lift three fingers in the air and shout "Serbia, Serbia." They stood on the side. Soldiers, the military, stood there. They were hitting us with whatever they had, with the rifles. I remember that a couple of lads fell down, that they were beating them. I received several blows myself, but nothing really very bad. I could run into the bus. And then we were all loaded on to those buses. I remember there was a driver in the bus and there was another armed soldier. They forced us to sing songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The people who were guarding the camp at Benkovac, could you tell if they were army, police, or what units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you got on the buses, was it the same guards? Was it army soldiers who were escorting you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I can't remember. We were not allowed to look very much in those bathrooms. We were isolated and we couldn't see what was happening outside or who there was. I'd never seen that man before. He was a soldier wearing camouflage uniform, so I don't know who that was. For me, he was just an unknown man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you're talking about the man you're talking about now, who was that? The driver of the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, the soldier who stood next to the driver, holding a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was the bus loaded fully? Was there the same number of passengers as seats?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was sitting at the back of the bus. I think they ordered us to bow our heads down. We were not supposed to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We rode on the bus. We didn't know where we were being taken to. Then the bus pulled over at some point. I can't remember how long we had been riding for up to that point, Benkovac, where the buses stopped. The bus was there for a while, and they made us get off the bus one by one. I was sitting at the back of the bus. When I came to the door to get off, I saw around ten soldiers. When I say, "soldiers," I'm referring to people wearing camouflage uniforms. I saw them beating a man. I just ran over very quickly and entered a garage. And there I mingled with the other people who were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you learn at that time where you had arrived, the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I think we didn't know where we were that evening. It was after nightfall, and as far as I can remember, no one really knew where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And later, did you learn and can you tell us now, where had you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Later, we learned that the place was Omarska, the mine, the iron ore mine Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the map for a moment, S51, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you were travelling on the bus, were you able to look out the window or not?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: There were blinds on the window so we couldn't see anything. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you, through your senses, your sense of the direction of the bus, your sense of smell, other senses, did you gain some belief as to where you had travelled to get to Omarska, of how you had gone?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, in those moments, at that time, I did not really myself think about the time because I was so scared and I had no idea what was in store for us. How much time had elapsed, I don't know. But at the time we set out, there was still daylight. And by the time we arrived, it was night. Whether it was an hour or more, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Looking at the map, S51, is there a road to Omarska, coming down from the mountain, that goes through Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there's a road which you can take to go from Kozarac to Mrakovica. Mrakovica is a memorial centre from World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you were travelling on the bus, did you smell anything?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was hot, with heavy rainfall, so the weather was quite volatile in those days. I can remember a strong smell on the bus, a strong smell of fire having been extinguished by water, a fire drowned out by water. So that was soon after we left Benkovac, and I assumed that we were passing through Kozarac. You could feel the strong smell of a fire drowned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you got to Omarska, you said that there were soldiers there when you got out of the bus. How were the soldiers lined up or how were they positioned, and what did the prisoners who left the bus have to do?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When we got off the bus, we had to do the same thing as when getting on to the bus. We ran directly from the bus into the garage where they put us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And while you were running, were the soldiers doing anything?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The soldiers were lined up on the sides, and they kept hitting us. So we ran as fast as we could, to avoid being hit. I remember that a man who was running ahead of me fell. He stumbled, and they started hitting him. I ran as fast as I could, and that was the only thing I could catch sight of. And then somehow he managed to reach the garage, too. And once we were all inside the garage, they closed the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what the conditions were like in that garage that you were kept in in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was just an ordinary garage, as far as I could notice, for cars to be kept in, and that's where they put us, all of us. There must have been around 150, 160 of us, or thereabouts. So there was not enough room inside this garage for us to sit down. We were all standing from that moment on, like sardines, packed like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in that garage with the group of about 150 men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I spent about ten days there. Ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was that like?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was dreadful. When they shut us up inside, it was very hot. There wasn't enough air. I remember that within half an hour or one hour, I was soaking with sweat. Everything I was wearing, my shirt, my trousers, it was all soaked in sweat. It was unbearable. I remember that I pressed my hand against the wall, and I saw that the paint on the wall began to melt. The ceiling was full of drops of sweat. Sweat was dripping from the ceiling. And then someone asked to have the window opened. I think someone did. I have no idea. But I remember that someone jumped up and smashed a window in order to get some air inside the room. But that didn't improve the situation because even after that, it was very stuffy and very hot. We asked for water because we were parched. And they said: "Okay, we'll give you some water but first you have to sing a song." So we sang at the top of our voices. And then a jerry can filled with water was brought to us, and then people started fighting over the jerry can. It was awful. It was a fight to survive, as simple as that. No one really cared about the person next to them. We fought like animals over the water they had brought us. It was really awful. I remember the first evening, two young men suffocated. I remember them very well. They were just lying there on the floor. They were dead. No one flicked an eye. No one paid any attention. That was the state we were in. And everyone just looked after himself. No one had any sympathy for the dead body lying there. Until a day ago, we had still talked to each other, and now this person was dead. But it made no difference. It was really awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During those ten days, were you fed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We arrived on Friday, and they gave us nothing until Sunday. They only threw jerry cans of water into the room. And then on Sunday, I remember clearly they opened the door and threw in some bread. And then there was chaos because people started struggling for that bread. Everyone was trying to get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to the two bodies of those that had died the first two days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The bodies were taken out and put on the grass there. I remember the following day, or perhaps after two days, they gave permission to go out to that lawn one by one so we could take a leak. And when I came out, I saw one of those dead lads lying there on the grass. How many days had elapsed in the meantime, two or three days perhaps. I can't remember. But I saw his body there on the lawn. I remember clearly what he looked like. He was bigger than me. He was quite tall, and he had curly hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said you arrived Friday night. When was it that you were let out of the room for the first time to urinate on the grass?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the next morning, but it was -- it was either Saturday morning or Sunday morning. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what you felt like when you were out there and saw the grass?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was perhaps 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning. It was a sunny day. I felt wonderful. The smell of the air was somehow pleasant, and the sunshine. It was nice. It's beyond words. It was a wonderful feeling. That was something, it's stuck in my memory, the morning and the grass, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the smell of fresh air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How had your life changed from one week earlier?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Unimaginably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How long were you in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I'm no longer clear about the dates, but the last group to leave Omarska, I was in that last group. We were transferred to Manjaca from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp, did you see any relatives?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I met my father, my uncle, my two cousins, my father's cousin, some neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about meeting your father.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: After about ten days, my name was called out. I went out, outside the garage, and they told me that I would be going for an interview. After the interview, they transferred me to a room, and my father was in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your father get called out of the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No. They showed me into the room and then I came in and saw that my father was there. I didn't even know that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to your father at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We were together in that room, for how long, a month, month and a half maybe. I can't say. They took him many times for questioning and they beat him many times. One day, they came, they called him out around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you rather finish this tomorrow? We have just a few more minutes today. Perhaps it would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.
